title: Alberta Votes 2026
eyebrow: Alberta provincial referendum · voting day Mon Oct 19, 2026

dates.mailBy: Vote-by-mail applications are closed; mailed ballots go to your returning office.

lede: Ten questions on ten separate ballots: one on whether to start down the road to a separation referendum, five on immigration, social programs and voter ID, and four on changing the Constitution. Read each one as it is worded, see what polls say, mark your own ballot, and compare it with Alberta's count as it comes in.
intro: Every voter gets the same ten ballots, handed out in this order, and can answer any or none of them. None of the results is binding: each asks the government to act, and most would need a new law, Ottawa, or other provinces to go further. Your answers stay on this page.

groups.label: Separation
groups.note: A choice between two options. Not binding.

groups.label: Immigration, programs and voter ID
groups.note: Yes or no. Not binding; each asks the government to write a law or seek more powers.

groups.label: The Constitution
groups.note: Yes or no. Each asks Alberta to seek a constitutional amendment with other willing provinces. Most amendments need Parliament plus at least seven provinces holding half the population; some need all ten.

questions.short: Remain a province, or start the process toward a binding separation referendum?
questions.q: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

options.full: Alberta should remain a province of Canada.
The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

questions.context: Option 2 would not take Alberta out of Canada. It asks the government to start the steps toward a later, binding referendum on separation. Under the Supreme Court's 1998 Secession Reference and the federal Clarity Act, separation would need a clear majority on a clear question, followed by negotiations with Ottawa and the other provinces.

questions.short: Take more control over immigration to lower it and prioritize economic migrants and Albertans for jobs?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?
questions.context: Immigration is a shared power under the Constitution, and federal law wins where the two conflict. Alberta already picks some economic immigrants through the Alberta Advantage Immigration Program, under an agreement with Ottawa. Taking more control would need a new agreement with the federal government, like the one Quebec has.

questions.short: Limit provincially funded programs to citizens, permanent residents and Alberta-approved statuses?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?
questions.context: Asks for a law limiting provincially funded programs such as health care, schools and social services to citizens, permanent residents and people whose immigration status Alberta approves. Today some temporary residents, such as many work-permit holders, qualify for some of these programs. The question leaves to a future law which statuses Alberta would approve.

questions.short: Make people with temporary status live in Alberta 12 months before getting provincial social supports?
questions.q: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?
questions.context: Asks for a law adding a 12-month Alberta residency wait before people with temporary immigration status, such as work or study permits, qualify for provincial social support programs. Citizens and permanent residents would keep the eligibility they have now.

questions.short: Charge people with temporary status a fee for their family's health care and schooling?
questions.q: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family's use of the healthcare and education systems?
questions.context: Would let the province charge people with temporary immigration status a fee or premium for their family's use of public health care and schools. Citizens and permanent residents would keep the access they have now. The question does not set an amount.

questions.short: Require proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate, to vote provincially?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?
questions.context: Today a voter shows ID proving who they are and where they live, and declares that they are a citizen. A Yes asks for a law requiring a citizenship document, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in provincial elections.

questions.short: Have provinces, not Ottawa, pick the judges of Alberta's King's Bench and Appeal courts?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King's Bench and Appeal courts?
questions.context: Under section 96 of the Constitution, Ottawa appoints the judges of each province's superior courts (in Alberta, the Court of King's Bench and the Court of Appeal). Provinces already appoint their own provincial court judges. A Yes asks Alberta to seek an amendment moving superior court picks to the provinces.

questions.short: Seek an amendment abolishing the unelected federal Senate?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?
questions.context: The Supreme Court ruled in 2014 that abolishing the Senate needs the consent of Parliament and all ten provinces. A Yes asks Alberta to pursue that amendment with other willing provinces. Alberta also holds its own Senate nominee elections, most recently in 2021.

questions.short: Let provinces opt out of federal programs in their areas without losing the federal money?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education, and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?
questions.context: Ottawa funds many programs in provincial areas, such as health care, through transfers that come with conditions. A province that stays out of a federal program generally gives up its share unless it negotiates a deal. A Yes asks Alberta to seek an amendment letting provinces opt out and keep the money for their own programs.

questions.short: Give provincial laws priority over conflicting federal laws in provincial and shared areas?
questions.q: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province's laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province's laws and federal laws conflict?
questions.context: Under the courts' rule of federal paramountcy, a valid federal law wins when it conflicts with a valid provincial law. A Yes asks Alberta to seek an amendment so that, in provincial and shared areas, the provincial law would win instead.

pollNote: Poll figures are shares of all respondents, undecided included, so a Yes figure leaves room for both No and undecided. Pollsters worded the questions differently. Compiled by Wikipedia and The Writ.
